# How tides arise

Along almost every coastline on Earth, the sea rises and falls twice within a day, climbing over rocks and sand for
a few hours and then retreating again, leaving behind a band of wet ground that marks how far the water reached.
People who live near the shore learn this rhythm without needing to be told what causes it: a boat left resting on
the mud at low water will be afloat again before the day is over, and a path along the rocks that is dry at one hour
will be submerged at another. The regularity of the pattern is what first draws attention to it. Long before anyone
could explain why the water moved in this way, sailors and fishing communities kept track of the timing, because a
harbor that could be entered easily at high water might be impossible to reach at low water, and a boat that set out
at the wrong moment could be stranded on a falling tide far from home.

The explanation for this rising and falling lies not in the sea itself but in the pull of other bodies in space,
chiefly the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun. Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass,
and the strength of that attraction weakens with distance. The Moon, though far smaller than the Sun, is so much
closer to the Earth that its gravitational influence on the oceans is more than twice that of the Sun. Because the
Earth is not a single point but a body of considerable size, the pull of the Moon is not felt equally everywhere on
it. The side of the Earth nearest the Moon feels a slightly stronger pull than the center of the Earth does, and the
side farthest from the Moon feels a slightly weaker pull than the center does. This difference between the pull felt
at different points is what physicists call a tidal force, to distinguish it from the overall gravitational pull,
which mostly just keeps the Earth and Moon orbiting one another.

The consequence of this difference is that the ocean is stretched very slightly along the line connecting the Earth
and the Moon, bulging outward both on the side facing the Moon and on the side facing away from it. It is a common
misunderstanding to think that the far-side bulge is somehow a shadow or a leftover effect; it arises for the same
reason as the near-side bulge, only in the opposite direction, because the far side of the Earth is being pulled
toward the Moon less strongly than the Earth's center is, and so relative to the center it lags behind, which looks,
from the Earth's own point of view, like an outward bulge. As the Earth rotates on its axis roughly once a day, a
given point on its surface passes through both of these bulges, which is why most coastlines see two high tides and
two low tides in about twenty-four hours and fifty minutes, the extra fifty minutes arising because the Moon itself
is slowly moving in its orbit around the Earth, so the Earth has to turn a little further each day to catch up to
the same position relative to the Moon.

The Sun contributes a tidal force of its own, weaker than the Moon's but still significant, and the two forces
combine depending on the relative positions of the Sun, Earth, and Moon. When the Sun and Moon are roughly aligned
with the Earth, either on the same side or on opposite sides, their tidal forces reinforce one another, producing
higher high tides and lower low tides than usual; these are called spring tides, a name that has nothing to do with
the season and everything to do with the water seeming to leap or spring up higher than at other times. This
alignment happens near the new moon and the full moon, roughly twice each lunar month. When the Sun and Moon are at
right angles to each other as seen from the Earth, which happens near the first and last quarter of the Moon, their
tidal forces partly cancel, producing what are called neap tides, when the difference between high and low water is
smaller than average. Anyone who watches the tides over the course of a month will notice this slow alternation
between larger and smaller swings, tracing out a rhythm layered on top of the daily rise and fall.

If the Earth were covered by a single uniform ocean with no continents interrupting it, the pattern of tidal
bulges would be simple to describe and would look much like a gentle, slow wave circling the globe twice a day.
The real ocean, however, is broken up by continents into separate basins, each with its own shape, depth, and size,
and water cannot simply flow uninterrupted around the planet. Instead, within each ocean basin, the tidal pull sets
up a much more complicated pattern of motion, one that depends heavily on the basin's geometry. Water sloshing
back and forth in a basin has natural periods of oscillation, much as water in a bathtub will slosh back and forth
at a particular rate depending on the tub's length and depth. When the natural period of a basin happens to be
close to the period of the tidal forcing, the response can be greatly amplified, a phenomenon called resonance.
This is part of why some places see enormous tidal ranges while others, not far away as the crow flies, see almost
none at all.

The most striking example of this amplification is found in certain bays and inlets with just the right shape and
depth to resonate strongly with the tide-generating forces. In such places, the difference between high and low
water can reach many meters, transforming the coastline twice a day: at low tide, a vast expanse of mud flats and
sandbars may stretch out where, a few hours later, boats will be floating freely. Fishing communities near such
bays have long organized their working days around this rhythm, timing the harvesting of shellfish or the movement
of boats to the hours when the flats are exposed or the channels are deep enough to pass. Visitors unfamiliar with
the local tides have sometimes been caught out by how quickly the incoming water can cut off a sandbar from the
shore, since the tide does not simply creep in evenly but can advance rapidly across a very gently sloping flat.

In sharp contrast, some seas that are nearly enclosed, connected to the wider ocean only through narrow straits,
show a very modest tidal range, sometimes just a few centimeters, because so little of the tidal energy from the
open ocean manages to propagate through the narrow connection, and because the basin's own size and depth put its
natural period far from that of the driving tidal forces. A traveler who has only experienced the modest tides of
such an enclosed sea might be startled the first time they encounter a coastline where the water's edge moves by
hundreds of meters between low and high tide.

Where a river meets the sea, the incoming tide can sometimes produce a distinctive traveling wave known as a tidal
bore, in which the leading edge of the rising tide advances up the river as a single abrupt front rather than as a
gradual rise. This tends to happen where a wide, funnel-shaped estuary narrows quickly as it meets a relatively
shallow river channel, concentrating the volume of incoming water into a shrinking cross-section so that it can no
longer spread out and instead piles up into a wave that pushes upstream against the river's normal flow. Some
tidal bores are barely noticeable ripples, while others form a wall of water substantial enough that people travel
specifically to watch it pass, timing their visit to the days near the spring tides when the bore is at its most
pronounced.

Tides are not only a matter of the sea's surface rising and falling in place; they also drive currents, since water
has to flow into a bay or estuary as the tide comes in and flow back out as it recedes. In narrow channels and
straits, these tidal currents can become quite fast, capable of moving vessels off their intended course if not
accounted for, and capable of stirring up sediment from the seabed, which is one reason why channels near strong
tidal currents often need to be dredged periodically to remain navigable. Sailors working in these waters have
traditionally needed to know not just the state of the tide, whether it is rising or falling, but also the state of
the tidal stream, since the two do not always change at exactly the same moment; there can be a delay between the
turning of the tide, as measured by the height of the water, and the turning of the current, as measured by the
direction water is flowing.

Because the timing of tides matters so much to those who work on or near the water, people have kept records of
tidal heights for centuries, noting the time and height of high and low water at particular ports, day after day,
year after year. These long records revealed that although the tide is driven by the regular motions of the Moon
and Sun, the response of any particular harbor is its own fixed pattern, repeating with remarkable consistency once
enough observations have been gathered. This discovery made it possible to predict future tides at a given port
from past records alone, without needing to calculate the underlying astronomical forces from scratch each time.
Tide tables, listing the expected time and height of high and low water at a harbor for months or years in advance,
became an essential tool for anyone whose work depended on the state of the water: harbor pilots guiding ships
through channels that were only deep enough at certain states of the tide, engineers planning work that could only
be done when a foundation was exposed at low water, and fishing crews deciding when to set out and when to return.

The construction of tide tables eventually moved from simple record-keeping toward a more systematic approach, in
which the complicated rise and fall of the water at a given port was treated as the sum of many simpler, regularly
repeating rhythms, each corresponding to some aspect of the relative motion of the Earth, Moon, and Sun: one rhythm
tied to the Moon's daily passage overhead, another to its monthly cycle of phases, another to the changing
distance between the Earth and the Moon over the course of that cycle, another to the Earth's own annual journey
around the Sun, and several others besides. By carefully measuring how strongly each of these rhythms showed up in
a harbor's tidal record, and how much each was delayed relative to the astronomical event that drove it, it became
possible to reconstruct the harbor's characteristic response and use it to predict tides far into the future. This
approach eventually allowed the predictions to be produced mechanically, first by purpose-built machines of gears
and pulleys designed to add together the many separate rhythms, and later by other means, but the underlying idea
remained the same throughout: treat the tide at a given place as a fixed pattern of response to a small number of
recurring astronomical rhythms, and let that pattern, once learned, speak for the future.

Tides are usually thought of in connection with the ocean, but the same gravitational forces act on any body of
water, and in principle even on the solid Earth itself and on the atmosphere above it. Large lakes do experience a
very small tidal rise and fall, though it is generally too small to notice without careful instruments, both
because the lake's water has much less room to be redistributed than an ocean basin does and because a lake's
much smaller size keeps it far from the kind of resonance that can amplify tidal motion in a well-shaped ocean bay.
The solid ground beneath our feet rises and falls by a small amount too, as the whole planet is very slightly
deformed by the same tidal forces that pull at the ocean, though this solid-earth tide, typically no more than a
few tens of centimeters, passes entirely unnoticed in the course of ordinary life. The atmosphere experiences
tides of its own as well, driven partly by gravitational pull and partly by the daily heating and cooling of the
air by sunlight, producing very small regular changes in atmospheric pressure that instruments can detect even
though no person could ever feel them directly.

The rise and fall of the tide also shapes the lives of the plants and animals that live along the shore, in ways
that have nothing to do with any human interest in the schedule. The zone of shoreline that is submerged at high
tide and exposed at low tide, known as the intertidal zone, is one of the most demanding environments on Earth for
a living creature to occupy, since anything living there must be able to withstand being underwater for part of the
day and exposed to open air, sun, and temperature swings for the rest of it. Many creatures of the intertidal zone
have developed shells that close tightly to hold in moisture during the hours of exposure, or the ability to burrow
into wet sand or mud to escape the drying air, or simply the patience to wait, clamped to a rock, for the water to
return. Birds that feed along the shore often time their foraging to the tide rather than to the clock, arriving at
the mud flats as the water recedes to search for creatures left behind or exposed by the retreating tide, and
moving on as the water rises again to cover the feeding ground. Watching such a shoreline through a full tidal
cycle reveals an entire community of organisms whose daily routines are set not by daylight, as for most living
things, but by the advance and retreat of the sea.

Human settlements near the coast have long had to reckon with the tide as a basic fact of geography, much as they
reckon with the slope of the land or the direction of the prevailing wind. Harbors were often built where the tidal
range and the shape of the coastline offered natural shelter and enough depth of water at least at high tide for
vessels to enter and leave safely. Some ports developed elaborate systems of gates and basins to hold water in
place after the tide receded, so that ships could remain afloat and cargo could be loaded and unloaded without
waiting for the tide to return. Bridges and causeways built across tidal channels had to account for the fact that
the same crossing might sit high and dry at one hour and be submerged by a fast-moving current a few hours later.
Even the placement of certain religious and civic sites near the coast has, in some traditions, been influenced by
the tide, whether for practical reasons of access or for the symbolic weight that the rhythm of the sea has carried
in the stories people tell about the passage of time.

Understanding tides also played an important part in the broader history of how people came to think about the
natural world as something governed by discoverable, repeating patterns rather than by unpredictable will. The
recognition that the tide, however locally complicated, ultimately traced back to the steady, calculable motions of
the Moon and Sun was one of the clearer early demonstrations that distant astronomical bodies could have a
measurable, everyday effect on events close to home. It offered a vivid and easily observed link between the
motions charted by astronomers, who had for a long time studied the sky mostly for its own sake or for calendars
and navigation, and a phenomenon that mattered immediately and materially to anyone who lived by the sea. That
link, once firmly established, encouraged the wider expectation that other apparently irregular natural phenomena
might likewise be traced back, with enough careful observation, to some steady underlying rhythm.

Today the tide is measured continuously at harbors around the world by instruments that record the height of the
water without needing a person to watch and note it down by hand, and the resulting long records are used both to
refine predictions for the years ahead and to detect slow changes in sea level that unfold over decades rather than
hours. Such records show that the average level of the sea at a given port can itself drift gradually over long
spans of time, for reasons quite separate from the familiar daily and monthly rhythm of the tide, and separating
this slow drift from the much larger and faster tidal swings requires exactly the same kind of careful, patient
analysis of repeating patterns that first allowed tide tables to be built centuries ago. In this way, the study of
the tide has never really stopped growing outward from its original, practical concern with the safe timing of a
boat's passage into harbor, even as its instruments and its questions have both changed a great deal since the
days when a fisherman judged the state of the water only by looking at how far it had crept up the beach that
morning.
